newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM apologises over "Stolen Generation".
newsitem.headline: Australian PM apologises over "Stolen Generation".

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard made an unexpected personal apology on Monday to tens of thousands of Aborigines taken from their parents under a past policy of forced assimilation.
Howard's apology came only a few hours before his government released a human rights watchdog report which said the forced assimilation amounted to genocide.

But Howard fell short of offering an official apology as called for by the Human Rights Commission in its report into the "Stolen Generation", Aborigines taken from their parents between the 1880s and the 1960s.

"Personally, I feel deep sorrow for those of my fellow Australians who suffered injustices under the practices of past generations towards indigenous people," Howard told a major conference in Melbourne on Aboriginal reconciliation.

"I am sorry for the hurt, the trauma, many here today may continue to feel as a consequence of those practices," Howard told a mainly hostile Aboriginal audience of around 1,500 delegates gathered to discuss strained black-white relations.
Howard won loud applause for his apology, but drew jeers when he said Australian history since white settlement in 1788 was not a history of "imperialism and exploitation and racism".
Hundreds of delegates stood and turned their back on Howard as he continued his speech, which stressed better Aboriginal living standards, not "gestures", was the key to reconcilation.
The 700-page report tabled in parliament contained a litany of physical and sexual abuse of Aborigines based predominately on a policy of white racial superiority.
"The Australian practice of indigenous child removal involved both systematic racial discrimination and genocide as defined by the international law," said the report entitled "Bringing them Home".
"Yet it continued to be practised as official policy long after being clearly prohibited by treaties to which Australia had voluntarily subscribed," the report added.

The rights watchdog said genocide did not necessarily mean the immediate physical destruction of a group or nation and that the forced removal of Aboriginal children was genocidal regardless of the good intentions of welfare groups at the time.
"A state can not excuse itself by claiming that the practice was lawful under its own laws or that its people did not (or do not) share the outrage of the international community," it said.
Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation chairman Pat Dodson welcomed Howard's personal apology but said the nation's parliament must follow suit. "It's a good start," Dodson said.

Parliamentarians in Canberra, including right winger Pauline Hanson, stood for a minute's silence out of respect for the Aborigines taken from parents as children between the 1880s and 1960s. Only one government MP refused to stand.
On Tuesday, Australia marks the 30th anniversary of a landmark referendum which gave Aborigines the right to vote. Until that they were governed under flora and fauna laws.
Aborigines stolen from their parents are demanding a formal apology and compensation, but the government has so far shied away from the question of compensation.
Dodson told the conference the outcome of the "Stolen Generation" issue and the government's stance on indigenous title to land were crucial to reconciliation with Aborigines.

"We can compensate for forcing people to hand in their guns and we now have to find a way to compensate those who were taken away (from parents)," said Dodson, referring to gun laws introduced after last year's mass killings in Tasmania state.
